notes.claim: A compound motor has both a series and a shunt field winding.
In a cumulative compound motor the series and shunt fields work together, with fluxes in the same direction; in a differential one they oppose.
A shunt coil added to a series motor limits the top speed at light load, and a cumulative compound motor has a definite no-load speed and can run safely with no load.
A cumulative compound motor has more starting torque than a shunt motor and steadier speed than a series motor, but not as steady as a shunt motor.
A differential compound motor is rarely used because it can run unstably when the load changes; because the series flux opposes the shunt flux, flux falls with load and the speed can rise with load.
A long-shunt connection puts the shunt winding across the supply with the series winding between it and the armature; a short-shunt connection puts the shunt winding across the armature only.
Compound motors suit presses, shears, crushers and reciprocating compressors.

NEMA defines a compound-wound motor as a direct-current motor with two separate field windings: one, usually the predominating field, connected as in a straight shunt-wound motor, and the other connected in series with the armature circuit.

Percent compounding is the share of the total field ampere-turns at full load that the series field contributes (NEMA). A stabilised-shunt motor takes about 3 to 10 percent from its series winding; one trade source says a typical industrial compound motor takes about 50 percent.

CONTESTED share: computed from the lesson's flux rule, a 50 percent series share would double the no-load speed, far outside the 15 to 30 percent speed regulation makers quote. The lesson uses a labelled example share (i8.examples.json) and does not teach 50 percent as a fact.

Flux rule for the picture: in a cumulative compound motor the series winding adds flux as the load current rises, so flux = shunt part + series part x armature current; in a differential one the series part is taken away (net flux falls with load). Speed follows applied voltage minus the armature-circuit drop, divided by net flux.

Cumulative: the series part supplies a large torque when the motor is started under a heavy load and the shunt part gives the constant-speed advantage of a shunt motor (US Navy training text). A compound motor has more torque than a shunt motor because of the series field, with a fairly constant speed because of the shunt field (DOE Fundamentals Handbook); it copes with heavy load changes better than a shunt motor because the extra current in the series coils strengthens the field (university notes).

Speed regulation of a cumulative compound motor is poorer than a shunt motor's: a load makes the speed fall further because the flux grows with load (PEG-3722; Engineers Edge says 'less speed regulation'). NEMA defines speed regulation as no-load minus rated-load speed, in percent of rated-load speed.

Makers' figures for a standard compound motor's speed regulation: about 30 percent (Baldor-Reliance, quoting NEMA MG1 12.65.2) and 15 to 25 percent (another Baldor-Reliance frame range). CONTESTED against his sheet, which says 'good speed regulation (like a shunt motor)': teach it as better than a series motor and worse than a shunt motor.

A compound motor is not suited to speed control by weakening its shunt field, because of the very high no-load speeds that can result (Baldor-Reliance). Its shunt part gives it a definite no-load speed and keeps it from running uncontrollably when the load goes (PEG-3722, existing sources 165 and 192).

Differential compound: the series field opposes the shunt field, so the net flux falls with load and the speed rises as the load increases, which may lead to instability. A heavy enough load can take the flux to zero so the machine stalls or reverses. It is rarely used (his sheet, existing source 190).

CONTESTED detail: PEG-3722 and Engineers Edge describe a differential motor as running at a constant speed with better regulation than a shunt motor. Both follow flux = shunt part - series part x current: a small series part only cancels the usual speed droop (flat), a large one makes the speed rise. The lesson teaches it as unstable (the sheet) and shows the rise in red.

Reversing the series field alone (or the shunt field alone) turns cumulative into differential; reversing both fields together does not change whether they aid or oppose. To reverse the direction of rotation of a compound motor, reverse the armature leads, or reverse both fields. A maker winds a motor as a straight shunt for regenerative drives, because the series winding would oppose the shunt winding when the motor is reversed or regenerates.

Fault to find after a repair or rebuild: a speed that climbs as armature current climbs points to a hidden differential series winding (a rebuild can reverse an internal series field), reversed interpole polarity or brushes off neutral. Check against the maker's connection diagram.

Safety and weight of evidence: do not find out the polarity by running the motor unloaded at normal voltage, because weak or opposing flux can allow excessive speed. One trade note adds that under high starting current a differentially connected series winding can overpower the shunt field and drive the motor the wrong way; one trade source only, so the lesson may say 'can' and no more.

Why a flywheel goes with a compound motor on a press or shear: the machine takes its working energy during the work stroke from the flywheel and the motor then brings the flywheel back to rated speed; flywheel kinetic energy is proportional to the square of its speed (Yaskawa; a university thesis says the same of the motor between punches).

A compound motor is generally used with a flywheel where sudden, temporary loads come on, as in rolling mills: the series winding takes the heavy load and the shunt winding stops dangerous speed when the load is suddenly removed. NO SOURCE says the speed droop is what lets the flywheel give up its energy; that follows from energy proportional to speed squared and is the lesson's own computed reasoning (i8.examples.json), said as such.

Uses: presses, shears and reciprocating machines are often driven by compounded motors (DOE Fundamentals Handbook; his sheet, existing source 201); a compound motor suits a reciprocating press or shear where a relatively consistent speed is wanted with irregular loads.

Long and short shunt (existing sources 199, 200): the lesson's drawing of his sheet is long shunt (shunt winding across the supply, series winding between it and the armature). Source gap: no source states the short-shunt current rule in quotable words, so the picture uses long shunt only.

Marine and naval line: the only support found is a US Navy training text (NEETS) describing the compound motor as one shunt winding in parallel with the armature and one series winding in series with it, with the speed and torque characteristics a combination of series and shunt motors. NO source was found that places a compound motor on a ship or names a shipboard compound-motor service, so the lesson carries no marine use line for the compound motor.

Example-set note: one worked tutorial uses a flux that changes by 0.4 percent for each ampere of armature current (240 V, 0.20 ohm). That is an example value, not a maker's; the lesson uses its own labelled per-unit set (i8.examples.json).
